episodes.177943: Isolated thunderstorms developed across portions of northern Illinois during the afternoon of April 19th, producing mainly large hail.
episodes.177945: Scattered thunderstorms moved across northern Illinois during the afternoon of April 20th producing large hail and wind damage.
episodes.177946: Scattered thunderstorms moved across southern Lake Michigan during the afternoon and evening of April 20th.
episodes.177960: A line of strong thunderstorms ahead of an approaching cold front produced hail and wind damage on the night of April 20 and early morning hours of April 21.
episodes.178017: One tornado was documented that moved north out of Chase county into far southeast Morris County around 905 pm CDT.   The tornado did damage to trees and one home before ending around 3 miles south southwest of Dunlap, Kansas.  Other storms produced large hail and damaging winds.  A second line of severe storms developed after midnight during the early morning hours of April 20th and produced wind damage most concentrated in Clay County in the city of Clay Center.
episodes.178125: A lone supercell thunderstorm moved from south central Kansas into central Kansas during the afternoon and evening of April 19th, 2023.  The cyclic storm produced very large hail up to 4 inches in diameter and numerous tornadoes across Chase county, Kansas.   Eight tornadoes formed from the supercell with the strongest producing EF2 damage.
episodes.178154: Broad troughing was present aloft across the Western US during the afternoon/evening of the 19th. An area of surface low-pressure slowly deepened and moved towards north-central Kansas, with dryline extending from central Kansas through western-north Texas by the late afternoon hours. A well-timed lead upper wave, combined with broken insolation, led to the development of a few supercell thunderstorms across central Oklahoma. Multiple instances of large to very large (>2 inches) hail, along with 18 tornadoes, occurred across central Oklahoma.
episodes.178302: Severe thunderstorms developed over central Oklahoma during the evening of the 19th, along and ahead of a dry line that extended through north central Oklahoma through southwestern Oklahoma. These storms moved into the western portions of eastern Oklahoma during the late evening. The air mass east of the dry line became very unstable during the afternoon. As a strong upper level disturbance approached the region from the west during the day, the lower and middle level wind fields strengthened, which resulted in strong deep-layer wind shear during the evening. The combination of instability and wind shear resulted in supercell thunderstorms, which produced hail up to grapefruit size in parts of eastern Oklahoma as they moved through the area.
episodes.178304: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed across northwestern Arkansas during the afternoon and evening of the 20th, along and ahead of a cold front that moved through the region. The strongest storms produced large hail up to half dollar size.
episodes.178424: A mid level ridge was weakening due to an approaching trough. This trough enhanced instability and showers across the region. Some of these showers resulted in waterspouts around Humacao and St. Thomas.
episodes.178483: An upper level low pressure system shifted east from Montana east into the Dakotas on April 20th, with the attendant trough extending southward through the Rockies before ejecting east through the Central and Southern Plains during the afternoon and evening. A strong southerly low level flow ahead of this trough ushered very warm and humid air back north into the Four State Region on the 19th-20th, which primed the area with moderate instability ahead of an associated cold front that entered the region during the afternoon. Large scale forcing increased by mid and late afternoon through the evening along and ahead of the front and upper trough within the warm, moist, and unstable sector, enhancing scattered to numerous shower and thunderstorm development across portions of East Texas, Southeast Oklahoma, and Southwest Arkansas. An isolated strong thunderstorm developed over Southern McCurtain County Oklahoma along the front, with nickel size hail reported in Haworth before weakening.
episodes.178484: An upper level low pressure system shifted east from Montana east into the Dakotas on April 20th, with the attendant trough extending southward through the Rockies before ejecting east through the Central and Southern Plains during the afternoon and evening. A strong southerly low level flow ahead of this trough ushered very warm and humid air back north into the Four State Region on the 19th-20th, which primed the area with moderate instability ahead of an associated cold front that entered the region during the afternoon. Large scale forcing increased by mid and late afternoon through the evening along and ahead of the front and upper trough within the warm, moist, and unstable sector, enhancing scattered to numerous shower and thunderstorm development across portions of East Texas, Southeast Oklahoma, and Southwest Arkansas. Multiple reports of damaging winds and large hail were observed, with an isolated tornado also touching down in Midtown Tyler in Smith County. Localized flash flooding was also reported on the Texas side of Texarkana before the storms weakened during the evening with the loss of heating and reduced instability.
episodes.178593: As a surface low pressure system tracked northwest of Illinois, semi-discrete thunderstorms developed ahead of a cold front. These storms produced scattered large hail, as well as damaging winds, across west-central and central Illinois. Storms weakened by late evening as they moved into eastern Illinois.
episodes.178620: An isolated severe thunderstorm moved east across the Ozark foothills during the warmest and most unstable hours of the afternoon. Hail up to quarter-size was reported with the storm. The storm occurred in warm moist south flow ahead of a cold front that trailed southwest from northwest Illinois across south central  and southwest Missouri.
episodes.178914: A severe thunderstorm producing large hail and high winds developed along a cold front as it moved across Milwaukee County.
episodes.179013: Early morning storms associated with a weakening low resulted in one stronger cell in central Iowa producing quarter sized hail before dawn. Later in the day, a deepening low across the central plains lifted into Iowa with storms developing along a dry line in the evening. These storms produced hail up to baseball sized, along with a brief tornado remained rural and did not cause any damage. Additional convection was reinvigorated overnight thanks to the low level et, but remained sub severe. Areas that received multiple rounds of storms saw two to three inches of much needed rain.
episodes.179144: During the afternoon-evening of the 19th, the entirety of South Central Nebraska remained safely to the west of a zone of severe thunderstorms that raked across parts of eastern Nebraska. However, the overnight hours briefly turned more active in southeast portions of the area, as the northern fringes of a complex of slightly-elevated, strong to severe storms swept across primarily parts of Webster, Nuckolls, Thayer and Fillmore counties between 12:30-2:30 a.m. CDT on Thursday the 20th. Although the most intense cells concentrated just south of the state line in Kansas, there was a lone, ground truth report of severe weather within South Central Nebraska: half dollar size hail in Superior shortly after 1:30 a.m. CDT. Already by 2:30 a.m. CDT, the back edge of what was now a small-scale quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) had departed local southeastern counties to the east, ending any severe storm threat for the night.||Turning to the meteorological situation, in short, this round of strong to severe storms was instigated by stout forcing/lift impinging upon a slightly-elevated frontal zone rooted around 850 millibars...positioned just to the cool side of a sharp surface front slicing southeastward across the region. Going into more detail, and starting with the bigger picture of the mid-upper levels, broad and seasonably-strong southwesterly flow overspread the Central Plains on the 19th, downstream from a large-scale trough/closed low centered over the MT/ND border region. At the surface, an initially slow-moving front stalled out slightly east of South Central Nebraska during the afternoon-evening, sparing the local area from the swath of severe storms that impacted eastern NE. However, as midnight loomed, a shortwave trough approached the area from the Central High Plains. At the surface, this upper disturbance caused low pressure to strengthen/consolidate over southwest KS by late evening (central pressure around 998 millibars). To the north of this low, a reinforcing cold front dove southeastward across South Central Nebraska during the evening, while just to the east of the area, the initial boundary that fired the afternoon convection began retreating northwestward a bit, effectively tightening up/sharpening a low level frontal zone aligned south-southwest to north-northeast from southwest KS into southeast NE. As the mid level wave intercepted the west edge of the instability axis rooted within the sharp elevated frontal zone based around 850 millibars, strong to severe storms rapidly flared up over north central Kansas around midnight CDT before brushing up into southeast portions of South Central Nebraska. Despite the local area residing just behind the surface front, the mesoscale environment was primed for slightly-elevated severe convection, as although most-unstable CAPE values were somewhat modest at only 500-1000 J/kg, effective deep-layer wind shear was quite vigorous at 50-60 knots.
episodes.179145: During the afternoon-evening of the 19th, this six-county North Central Kansas area remained safely to the west of a zone of severe thunderstorms that raked across parts of south central and eastern Kansas. However, the overnight hours turned more active as a cluster of slightly-elevated, strong to severe storms swept across primarily Osborne, Mitchell, Smith and Jewell counties between 12-2 a.m. CDT on Thursday the 20th, prompting a few reported instances of large hail up to tennis ball size and unofficially-measured winds up to 67 MPH. Storms first erupted over the Rooks-Osborne County line and up into Smith County between 12:00-12:30 a.m. CDT. The southern-most cell quickly became severe, prompting accounts of ping pong ball to tennis ball size hail in far southern Osborne County and also a report of golf ball size stones near Hunter in Mitchell County. By 1 a.m. CDT, another storm over Jewell County reached severe levels, dropping quarter size hail in Mankato. As for winds, several area mesonet clocked primarily sub-severe gusts in the 45-55 MPH range. However, one unofficial personal weather station on the north side of Beloit registered gusts as high as 67 MPH (there were no known reports of wind damage). By 2 a.m. CDT, the back edge of what was now a small-scale quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) had departed North Central Kansas to the east-northeast, ending any local severe storm threat for the night. ||Turning to the meteorological situation, in short, this round of strong to severe storms was instigated by stout forcing/lift impinging upon a slightly-elevated frontal zone rooted around 850 millibars...positioned just to the cool side of a sharp surface front slicing southeastward across the region. Going into more detail, and starting with the bigger picture of the mid-upper levels, broad and seasonably-strong southwesterly flow overspread the Central Plains on the 19th, downstream from a large-scale trough/closed low centered over the MT/ND border region. At the surface, an initially slow-moving front stalled out slightly east of North Central Kansas during the afternoon-evening, sparing the local area from the swath of severe storms that impacted south central/eastern KS. However, as midnight loomed, a shortwave trough approached the area from the Central High Plains. At the surface, this upper disturbance caused low pressure to strengthen/consolidate over southwest KS by late evening (central pressure around 998 millibars). To the north-northwest of this low, a reinforcing cold front dove southeastward across North Central Kansas during the evening, while just to the east of the area, the initial boundary that fired the afternoon convection began retreating northwestward a bit, effectively tightening up/sharpening a low level frontal zone aligned south-southwest to north-northeast through the heart of Kansas. As the mid level wave intercepted the west edge of the instability axis rooted within the sharp elevated frontal zone based around 850 millibars, the North Central Kansas storms rapidly flared up during the midnight (CDT) hour. Despite the local area residing just behind the surface front, the mesoscale environment was primed for slightly-elevated severe convection, as although most-unstable CAPE values were somewhat modest at only 500-1000 J/kg, effective deep-layer wind shear was quite vigorous at 50-60 knots.
episodes.179217: An enhanced risk resulted in a widespread large hail event across southeast Nebraska. Storms developed after 4 PM along a stationary front near the Nebraska/Kansas border. A total of 55 storm reports were sent out by the office, most of which were for hail. The largest hailstone reported was 3 inches near Nebraska City. In addition to the hail, there were 4 observed tornadoes in OAX's Iowa counties.
episodes.179221: An enhanced risk resulted in a numerous hail event across southwest Iowa. Storms developed after 4 PM along a stationary front near the Nebraska/Kansas border and moved into Iowa. A total of 55 storm reports were sent out by the office, most of which were for hail. The largest hailstone reported was 3 inches near Thurman. In addition to the hail, there were 3 observed tornadoes. Two in Fremont County and one in Pottawatomie County.
episodes.179260: Strong to severe storms developed over southwest Missouri during the early afternoon and moved eastward into central and south central Missouri as a cold front moved across the region and interacted with an unstable airmass. Hail up to the size of golf balls occurred over Taney County, and wind gusts over 60 mph were measured at the Springfield-Branson National Airport.
episodes.179573: A severe thunderstorm producing large hail and high winds moved across Milwaukee County. The large hail was confined inland from Lake Michigan. However, wind damage was reported within 1 mile of Lake Michigan as the storms moved out and over the open waters.
episodes.179603: An upper level trough moved across the southwest US and brought a cold front through Central Texas. Thunderstorms developed in the warm, moist airmass south of the front in response to a mid-level shortwave trough. Some of these storms produced severe weather including one tornado.
episodes.179622: There was nearly a week between storm systems with temperatures again warming into the 80s from the 17th through the 20th across much of the state. Before cool temperatures were seen across the state, a couple more rounds of thunderstorms were expected. The first of which took place from April 20-22. A few reports of severe weather were received with some locally very heavy rainfall observed as well. Little Rock received more than 3 inches of rain in a 24 hour period. A lightning strike occurred very close to the NWS office in North Little Rock on the evening of April 20th which damaged some equipment.
episodes.179672: A deepening low pressure system over the area resulted in storm force east wind gusts at Passage Island Light on the evening of the 20th.
episodes.179752: A powerful storm system moved across eastern Iowa into southwest Wisconsin, sweeping a strong cold front through the area during the afternoon hours of Thursday, April 20th. A line of thunderstorms developed quickly along the front, with one of these storms becoming severe in Clark County as it neared the Mississippi River.
episodes.179754: A powerful storm system moved across eastern Iowa into southwest Wisconsin, sweeping a strong cold front through the area during the afternoon hours of Thursday, April 20th. A line of thunderstorms developed quickly along the front, with some of them becoming severe and producing hail in the counties along Mississippi River in eastern Iowa.
episodes.179759: A powerful storm system moved across eastern Iowa into southwest Wisconsin, sweeping a strong cold front through the area during the afternoon hours of Thursday, April 20th. A line of thunderstorms developed quickly along the front, with some of them surpassing severe thresholds producing hail up to the size of a golf ball.||An EF1 tornado tracked to the northeast for about 6 miles starting just east of Morrison, IL just before 3 PM CST.
episodes.179783: A strong cold front moved through the region during the afternoon hours. There was a narrow corridor of 1000 to 2000 J/kg of MLCAPE along and ahead of the cold front where dewpoints reached the low 60s. This instability, combined with deep-layer wind shear of 30 to 40 kts, supporting organized thunderstorms. There were numerous reports of large hail and some damaging winds with the severe storms.
episodes.179784: A strong cold front moved through the region during the afternoon hours. There was a narrow corridor of 1000 to 2000 J/kg of MLCAPE along and ahead of the cold front where dewpoints reached the low 60s. This instability, combined with deep-layer wind shear of 30 to 40 kts, supporting organized thunderstorms. There were numerous reports of large hail and some damaging winds with the severe storms.
episodes.179807: Storms brought hail to eastern KS on the evening of April 19th and the early morning of April 20th.
episodes.179811: A storm in Kirksville caused some wind damage.
episodes.179885: During the evening of April 19th, a cold front passed through Northwestern Kansas that produced damaging wind gusts up to 70 mph in the region. Blowing dust was also reported in the region due to these high winds that reduced visibilities down to near zero in some locations. An isolated thunderstorm also developed within the region due to the cold front passage that yielded hail up to a penny in size.
episodes.179923: Isolated supercell thunderstorms developed in the evening around Abilene along a well defined dryline. The storms produced many reports of large to very large hail.
episodes.179971: A strong spring storm affected much of Wisconsin in the middle of April, providing upwards of 20 of snow in north-central Wisconsin on an already deeper than average snowpack. Subsequent anomalously warm temperatures resulted in a rapid melt of this deep snowpack and rapid rises along the Black River in Central Wisconsin. The highest above flood stage occurred at Black River Falls reaching 6.42 ft above flood stage on April 21st. The combination of this strong spring storm and subsequent flooding impacts resulted in the Governor of Wisconsin declaring a State of Emergency on April 16th.
episodes.180003: An upper trough moving through the Southern Plains generated scattered to numerous thunderstorms across North and Central Texas on Thursday April 20. Storms were focused along a slow-moving cold front, and several of them became severe with large hail being the primary severe weather occurrence. Hail up to 2 inches was reported in Coryell County and hail up to 3 inches was reported in Collin County.
episodes.180034: The spring snowmelt flooding began in late April 2023 and persisted into the early portions of May for some locations.
episodes.180039: Spring snowmelt flooding began in mid to late April in most locations, then persisted into early May.
episodes.180044: Snowmelt flooding along the North Dakota Tributaries began in early to mid-April, with a few locations persisting into early May.
episodes.180050: Isolated to scattered thunderstorms developed across portions of the Heartland into the northwest Hill Country along a cold front and a dryline. Isolated severe thunderstorms produced large hail.
episodes.180161: A weak upper-level wave moving through southwest flow aloft, acting on an environment with 1000 to 1500 J/kg of MUCAPE in the vicinity of a surface trough, resulted in scattered thunderstorms across far southeast South Dakota, far northeast Nebraska, northwest Iowa, and southwest Minnesota during the evening of April 19th. The strongest storms produced severe hail ranging from 1.0 to 1.5 inches in diameter.
episodes.180162: A weak upper-level wave moving through southwest flow aloft, acting on an environment with 1000 to 1500 J/kg of MUCAPE in the vicinity of a surface trough, resulted in scattered thunderstorms across far southeast South Dakota, far northeast Nebraska, northwest Iowa, and southwest Minnesota during the evening of April 19th. The strongest storms produced severe hail ranging from 1.0 to 1.5 inches in diameter.

The strongest storms produced severe hail ranging from 1.0 to 1.5 inches in diameter.

events.narrative: Relayed via emergency manager.
Trained spotter reported quarter sized hail cover the ground in Ute.

The first tornado out the April 19th outbreak developed southeast of SE 89th Street and Sooner Road and moved north-northeast crossing into Oklahoma County. In Cleveland County, trees and a shed were damaged.
Photos shared on social media showed quarter size hail near 9000 North Road and 3500 West Road, west of Manteno.

The first tornado of the outbreak moved into Oklahoma County from Cleveland County. The tornado moved north-northeast with the east edge of the tornado brushing Air Depot Blvd before turning northwest and dissipating north of SE 59th Street between Sooner Road and Air Depot Blvd. Roof damage occurred at an industrial building along Air Depot Blvd, and a number of storage pods there were blown around by the tornado.
Trained spotter reported 1-inch hail.
MPing report.
This was reported via mPing.

Multiple photos, videos, and reports confirm that a brief 30-second-long ground circulation developed below a long-lived funnel cloud in this approximate location, lofting dust or light debris. No damage was reported or surveyed with this tornado.
Delayed report via social media, time estimated by radar.
MPing report.
MPing report.
Half dollar sized hail reported.
Report of 60 mph wind gust.

The second tornado of the outbreak developed along County Road 1340 about 1.5 miles west of the Grady-McClain County line. The tornado moved east along County Road 1340 destroying a small trailer and a small shed, and damaging trees and a power pole. The tornado moved into McClain County.
Significant car damage was reported.
MPing report.

The second tornado of the outbreak moved into McClain County from Grady County along County Road near Sunny Side Road. it moved east along Sunny Side road causing tree damage and roof damage to at least one home before turning southeast and then south-southeast and damaging another home roof and destroying a carport as it crossed State Highway 76.
Hail 0.88 inch in diameter fell 1 mile south-southeast of Ponca.
MPing report.
Hail 1.0 inch in diameter fell in Ponca.

The third tornado of the outbreak, the Cole-Goldsby Tornado, was the most destructive of the outbreak. The multiple-vortex tornado touched down near Rockwell Avenue south of 260th Street and moved in an erratic path, generally east and east-northeast through Cole. Many homes and mobile homes were damaged or destroyed near and in Cole. A man was killed in a destroyed mobile home in the far western portion of Cole. A woman was injured in a nearby mobile home, but died of a heart attack on the way to the hospital (indirect fatality). EF3 rated damage was found to at least three homes on Portland Avenue and Main Street in Cole with most exterior walls removed.||After moving through Cole and crossing State Highway 74B, the tornado continued to move northeast, then becoming narrower and turning northerly as it past 290th Street/Chestnut Road, moving between Western Avenue and Santa Fe Avenue just west of the town of Goldsby and dissipating before reaching State Highway 9. It continued to produce roof damage (up to EF2) to homes and tree damage.

A strong spring storm in the middle of April provided over 20 of snow on a deeper than average snowpack in north-central Wisconsin, quickly followed by anomalously warm temperatures and rapid melting. The Black River at Black River Falls rapidly rose above flood stage and crested at 53.42 ft on April 21st, 6.42 ft above flood stage.
Trained spotter reported 1.75-inch hail.
Public reported 1.75-inch hail.
Gustnado reported southwest of 29th and Glick Road.
The fourth tornado of the outbreak caused tree and power pole damage west of Cole between State Highway 76 and Rockwell Avenue north of 260th Street.
MPing report.
COOP observer reported 1-inch hail near Du Bois.
MPing report.
Public reported 1-inch hail.
Hail in Elk Point ranged from 1.0 to 1.5 inches in diameter.
Hail 1.5 inches in diamater fell in Cleghorn.
Reported at 29th and Glick Road.
Quarter size hail fell in Elk Point.
MPing report.

While the Cole-Goldsby tornado was still ongoing, the fifth tornado of the outbreak developed to the south. This tornado touched down just northwest of 260th Street and Fernwood Road, initially moving southeast then curving northeast dissipating southeast of Santa Fe Avenue and State Highway 74B. The tornado partially unroofed a home, heavily damaged an outbuilding, and produced tree damage along the path.
Public reported 1.25-inch hail via mPING.

Over an approximately 20-minute period, several hail reports were received from in and near Nebraska City. The largest stone was 3-inches reported by the public. The Emergency Manager relayed several reports of golf ball sized hail across the town.
Occasional hail up to quarter size fell 8 miles south of Arthur.
Trained spotter reported 1.5-inch hail.
Public reported 1.25-inch hail.

The Washington-Slaugherville tornado, the sixth of the outbreak, formed on the east edge of Washington and moved east and northeast crossing Interstate 35, and then crossing the Canadian River into Cleveland County due west of Slaugherville. In McClain County, a few homes suffered roof damage, and numerous trees along the path were damaged.
Storm Chasers had video of this tornado as it remained in rural areas of Crawford county between Deloit and Schleswig.  The tornado did not impact any damage indicators, hence the EFU rating.

While observing the Washington-Slaughterville Tornado, a storm chaser observed another tornado north of State Highway 74. An NWS Damage Survey Team found a path of damaged trees, power poles and fences. This was the seventh tornado of the outbreak.
MPing report.
Delayed report, time estimated by radar. Severely damaged cars with ground covered in hail.
MPing report.
Spotters reported a funnel cloud and were unsure of tornado development at time of report.
Hail 1.0 inch in diameter fell 7 miles southeast of Westfield.
MPing report.

The Washington-Slaugherville Tornado moved into Cleveland County from McClain County moving northeast, then turned east-southeast dissipating just west of 60th Street and Slaugherville Road. The damage in Cleveland County was primarily to tree branches.
MPing report.
MPing report.
Broadcast media reported hail 1.25 inches in diameter, resulting in cars pulling off Interstate 29.
MPing report.

This is the first tornado which a storm survey revealed that an outbuilding was thrown 250 yards. Additional outbuildings were collapsed on site. The roof of a silo was removed from the top, and walls at the base were pushed in. This was rated an EF1 tornado.
Hail 1.0 inch in diameter fell 7 miles east-southeast of Westfield, lasting for 5 minutes.
Time was estimated via radar.
Hail 1.0 inch in diameter fell 5 miles west-northwest of Sioux City.
Multiple photographs and reports from storm chasers and public confirm a brief tornado near this location. No damage was reported or surveyed.

The second tornado of the event was found following assessment of drone footage courtesy of Chase County Sheriff. This brief tornado damaged two farm outbuildings with parts of the roof torn off and was rated an EF0.
MPing report.

This is the third tornado which initially caused the loss of roof material on an outbuilding. The tornado crossed U.S. Highway 50, and a semi was blown over resulting in one injury. Several small road signs were taken out. A one to two foot diameter tree was snapped before the tornado lifted. This tornado was rated an EF0.
Time was estimated via radar.
The public reported tennis ball size hail 3 miles of Dyess AFB.
MPing report.
MPing report.
MPing report.

The fourth tornado had a peak width of a half mile wide and was rated EF2. It caused the metal posts of an outbuilding to be twisted and scattered leaving the structure leaning. There was total destruction to a couple of outbuildings as well as significant tree damage.
MPing report.
Penny to quarter sized hail with ponding of water on roads in town.
Report via mping.
Public reported 1-inch hail.
Multiple photographs and accounts from storm chasers and public confirm a tornado in this approximate location that lasted for approximately 3 minutes. No damage was reported with this tornado.
Public reported 1.25-inch hail.
MPing report.
Public report relayed by broadcast media. Time and location estimated by radar.
Public reported 1-inch hail via mPING.
The was the fifth tornado of the event. It tracked just north of Chase County Lake and damage was limited to trees and small outbuildings.

The eighth tornado of the outbreak, and the first of four tornadoes in the Etowah OK area touched down along Cemetery Road between 108th and 120th Streets. The tornado moved east-northeast damaging trees and unroofing one barn.
The sixth tornado produced by the supercell tracked across the town of Cottonwood Falls producing EF1 damage, mainly to trees and minor damage to roof structures.

The ninth tornado developed soon after the eighth dissipated, developing southeast of 120th Avenue and Maguire Road. The tornado moved erratically east and northeast dissipating near 180th Avenue between Etowah Road and Post Oak Road. Multiple mobile homes were destroyed and numerous homes suffered roof damage with the most intense damage along Maguire Road. Numerous trees were damaged along the path as well and two RVs were flipped over.
Delayed report, time estimated via radar.
This was the seventh tornado of the event. Damage was limited to trees and siding of homes.
Hail 1.0 inch in diameter fell in Merrill.
MPing report.
Corrects previous report 3 west of Strong City.
MPing report.

Tornado #10 occurred simultaneous to and somewhat parallel to tornado #9 to the south of Etowah. This tornado moved east just north of Maguire Road developing near 156th Avenue. At least two large barns were destroyed as well as numerous trees along the path.
MPing report.
MPing report.

This was the eighth tornado documented by the NWS Wichita damage Survey Team. This tornado mainly produced EF0 damage to mainly trees.  There was one minor injury close to the initial touchdown along Highway 50, when a car was thrown 30 yards off the highway.  The person was treated and released.
MPing report.
This was reported via social media.

The eleventh tornado of the outbreak, and the fourth of four in the Etowah area, developed a minute or two after tornado #9 dissipated. This tornado developed near 180th Avenue and Post Oak Road and quickly become a very wide tornado as it moved north-northeast, and then northeast before crossing into Pottawatomie County just south of Lindsey Street. Numerous EF2 rated points were observed during the first two miles of the tornado path including significant damage to homes and destruction of mobile homes.
MPing report.
Report from mping of small tree limbs broken or shingles blown off.
MPing report.
This was the ninth and final tornado of the event. It caused damage to transmission powerlines before crossing into Topeka's County Warning Area and causing minor damage to a home.
A funnel cloud was spotted by Dyess AFB weather observer.
Half dollar sized hail reported.
The public reported baseball size hail at Kirby Lake, just south of Loop 322.

This eleventh tornado moved into Pottawatomie County from Cleveland County, crossing the county line just south of Lindsey Street/Little River Road. The tornado was becoming narrower quickly as it crossed the county line, from a maximum of 2200 yard width in Cleveland County to about 750 yards wide as it crossed the county line and continued to become narrower until dissipating about 3/4 mile after moving into Pottawatomie County. A home and a mobile home had shingle and siding damage, and trees and power poles were also damaged.
The public reported tennis ball size hail 1 mile east of Kirby Lake.
MPing report.

Results of an NWS damage survey revealed tree damage and damage to a home approximately 3 miles SSW of Dunlap, Kansas. The home had portions of the roof removed and windows broken. This appeared to be the end of the tornado track that moved north out of Chase County.  The tornado appears to have crossed from Chase into Morris County around 905pm and ended around 908 pm CDT based on radar data.  Based on DOD to DI winds estimated to be around 95 mph.

The twelfth tornado of the outbreak developed about 2 miles south-southeast of Pink. This tornado was very slow, moving only 0.6 mile in 5 minutes near the intersection of Okay Road and Willow View Road. A metal truss electric transmission tower collapsed in the tornado and is the source of the EF3 rating. The tornado also damaged at least two homes and numerous trees.
The public reported hen egg size hail just southwest of Abilene Regional Airport.
Hail 1.0 inch in diameter fell in Remsen.
Golf ball sized hail reported.
The thirteenth tornado of the outbreak touched down briefly in east Norman, along Geronimo Drive, northwest of 108th Avenue NE and Alameda Drive. An outbuilding and trees were damaged.
Emergency manager reported 1-inch hail.
MPing report.
Hail 1.0 inch in diameter fell in Rock Valley.

The fourteenth tornado of the outbreak developed north of Pink southeast of the intersection of Walker Road and Waco Road, and moved north-northwest and then northwest before moving into Cleveland County south of Lake Road. In Pottawatomie County, a number of homes, mobile homes and a church were damaged by the tornado with at least one home where the entire roof was removed.
MPing report.

The fifteenth tornado of the outbreak developed northeast of Little Axe southwest of the intersection of 180th Avenue SE and Tecumseh Road and moved northeast dissipating east of this intersection. Trees were downed and one home on Tecumseh Road suffered roof damage.
Hail 1.5 inches in diameter fell in Doon.

The fourteenth tornado of the outbreak moved into Cleveland County from Pottawatomie County just south of Lake Road (Pottawatomie County)/SE 134th Street (Cleveland County) and moved northeast for over a mile. In Cleveland County, the damage was primarily to trees.

A tornado developed in Bethel Acres near Bethel Road south of Clear Pond Road, and moved north-northwest dissipating northwest of the intersection of Bethel Road and Lake Road. The Shawnee Tornado was the seventeenth tornado of this outbreak. This large, mulitple-vortex tornado initially developed near New Hope Road and Gaddy Road just southeast of Bethel Acres. It moved northeast quickly become a large tornado with a width of up to 1.3 miles. The tornado moved northeast into Shawnee, then turned north moving through western and northern portions of Shawnee with damage at Oklahoma Baptist University, areas near the Shawnee Mall near Interstate 40 and Kickapoo Street, and numerous locations in Shawnee. The large tornado continued north and north-northwest producing damage along both Kickapoo Street and Leo Road all the way north to the Lincoln County line. The tornado moved into Lincoln County just west of Kickapoo Street and dissipated soon after.

An isolated tornado began just east of Morrison IL around 2:56 PM CST. The tornado damaged a power pole and a tree at this location. The tornado then caused sporadic damage until it approached Fulfs Road.  It strengthened at this location and caused damage to trees, farm outbuildings, and a power pole. The tornado ended shortly after this location. Wind speeds are estimated in the 105-110 MPH range, with a rating of EF1. At it's widest, the tornado was 300 yards and was likely a multi-vortex tornado. The tornado path length was nearly 6 miles.
